stanzas: Deo gratias Anglia redde pro victoria!
Owre kynge went forth to Normandy,
With grace and myzt of chivalry;
The God for hym wrouzt marvelously,
Wherefore Englonde may calle, and cry
Deo gratias:
Deo gratias Anglia redde pro victoria.
He sette a sege, the sothe for to say,
To Harflue toune with ryal aray;
That toune he wan, and made a fray,
That Fraunce shall rywe tyl domes day.
Then went owre kynge, with alle his oste,
Thorowe Fraunce for all the Frenshe boste;
He spared ‘for’ drede of leste, ne most,
Tyl he come to Agincourt coste.
Than for sothe that knyzt comely
In Agincourt seld he sauzt manly,
Thorow grace of God most myzty
He had bothe the felde, and the victory.
Ther dukys, and erlys, lorde and barone,
Were take, and slayne, and that wel sone,
And some were ledde in to Lundone
With joye, and merthe, and grete renone.
Now gracious God he save owre kynge,
His peple, and all his wel wyllynge,
Gef him gode lyfe, and gode endynge,
That we with merth mowe savely synge
Deo gratias:
Deo gratias Anglia redde pro victoria.
orig.credit: Anonymous (15th century), as printed in Thomas Percy's Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765)
orig.page: Reliques of Ancient English Poetry/Volume 2/For the Victory at Agincourt

stanzas: England, give thanks to God for victory!
Our king went forth to Normandy
with grace and might of chivalry;
God worked marvellously for him there,
wherefore England may call and cry:
Thanks be to God:
England, give thanks to God for victory.
He laid a siege, to tell the truth,
to Harfleur town with royal array;
that town he won, and made a fight
that France shall rue till doomsday.
Then went our king, with all his host,
through France, for all the French boast;
he held back for fear of neither least nor greatest
till he came to the Agincourt coast.
Then, in truth, that comely knight
fought manfully on Agincourt field;
through the grace of God most mighty
he had both the field and the victory.
There dukes and earls, lord and baron,
were taken and slain, and that right soon,
and some were led into London
with joy and mirth and great renown.
Now gracious God, may he save our king,
his people, and all who wish him well;
give him good life and a good ending,
that we with mirth may safely sing:
Thanks be to God:
England, give thanks to God for victory.

notes: A plain modern rendering of the 15th-century English, made line by line from Percy’s text.
Percy prints z for the old letter yogh (myzt = might, wrouzt = wrought) and "seld he sauzt" for "feld he faught" (field he fought).
In the manuscript the Latin refrain follows every stanza; Percy marks it "Deo gratias, &c.", left out here.
